Nice way to think about it.

I guess it really depends on the severity of the defect. Would it allow some really significant exploit? -> Important to fix.

Does the defect only prohibit one very esoteric use-case which basically never comes up (and was thus never reported by a human user and only now that we have an infinitely patient machine checking every completely unlikely code path is it detected) -> more productive use of your time to develop a new feature which would be used by more people.

You don't want to fix them all because every fix has an opportunity cost. This was the big shift of switching language from "bug" to "defect".

Logically, a bug that prevents someone from doing something and a missing feature that prevents someone from doing something are equivalent, they shouldn't be thought of as two separate activities but should be evaluated via the same framework. The list of all defects in a piece of software is infinite so it becomes impossible to erase all defects. It's about prioritizing with finite resources.

> You can't predict the harm from a small bug when AI can chain complex exploits and when your software is used in mission critical applications as a data store.

Yes, any bug can theoretically be part of an exploit chain, just like any tumor detected can theoretically be the tumor that kills you. This is why the detection paradox exists. Once you become aware of the tumor, you face a duty to try and mitigate it. But we know from autopsies that people die with all sorts of tumors that didn't kill them.

Similarly, if we bothered to do autopsies of software products after sunsetting to discover a comprehensive list of CVEs, we'd discover a ton of bugs we were better off not knowing about because they ended up not making an impact but we would have diverted resources if we knew about them.

children.text: The word "generally" contains a lot of assumptions in that first sentence. I can think of a couple of scenarios where fixing a bug can absolutely spiral. There are even cases where the far better outcome is to leave a bug in place now that it is known.

It is generally easy to fix a bug that has already be found and can be reproduced (has been diagnosed, so to speak) than to find that bug in the first place. That's one of the reasons that LLM security scanning has become so important recently: it massively reduces the cost of finding those vulnerabilities.

As to your second point, you don't know exactly what a person will die of, but you can make statically sound estimates. You generally won't test unlikely potential causes of death (either because the chance of a positive result is too small, or because you know there are other, more serious conditions). But once a vulnerability is known, it is infinitely reproducible, which means the chance of the vulnerability being "fatal" (assuming the conditions exist for it to be exploited) is essentially 1.

The other flaw in the analogy is that in medicine, the patient chooses to do the tests on themselves. But in software security, there is an adversarial attacker as well as the "doctor" trying to defend the software. And in general, if the defender can find a vulnerability, they must assume that an attacker could already have found the same vulnerability (because the attacker and defender have largely the same tools and information at their disposal, especially in open source contexts), in which case, as discussed previously, that vulnerability also needs to be assumed to be fatal.

> Firstly, the cost of fixing a bug once you know it exists is usually minimal compared to the cost of discovering that bug.

Boy, I wish!

> Like you say, you typically only die of one thing, so if you know the patient won't die of a particular diagnosis because something else is more likely to kill them, then it might not be worth making that diagnosis.

You can't know someone didn't die of X until after they died, that's the entire point of this dilemma.

That's a flawed analogy though.

Firstly, the cost of fixing a bug once you know it exists is usually minimal compared to the cost of discovering that bug. This is the inverse of medicine, where the cost of testing (at least in terms of health outcomes for the patient) is typically minimal compared to the cost of treatment.

Secondly, if you have an asymptomatic illness, this does not typically make you more vulnerable (hence why it's asymptomatic). Like you say, you typically only die of one thing, so if you know the patient won't die of a particular diagnosis because something else is more likely to kill them, then it might not be worth making that diagnosis. But for software, you can be simultaneously vulnerable to lots of things at once, and any of these vulnerabilities can be the one to "kill" you. Some vulnerabilities may be easier to find and exploit (or do more damage) but in principle any active vulnerability can be exploited.

Thirdly, having multiple vulnerabilities makes software more vulnerable overall, because those vulnerabilities can potentially be chained together to create more serious exploits than each vulnerability would have represented on its own. To a certain extent this can be true in medicine as well, but generally it isn't.

Fourthly, we can't cure death (yet?) but we can cure all the vulnerabilities that we've found so far. There is no known upper bound on the lifespan of a piece of software, and we know that older code tends to have fewer bugs in that newer code, presumably because those bugs have been fixed over time. This is different from health issues, where a given condition may be chronic or terminal and therefore at a certain point there's nothing you can do to fix it.

Finally, ultimately in healthcare it's your body, and your decision was to what you do with it (assuming you can find a doctor willing to do what you want). If you have a condition and you want it cured, even if it is completely benign and will have no impact on your life whatsoever, then you can do that. (Again, assuming you have the resources and the condition is curable). But a software vulnerability does not affect you as the developer of the software, it instead affects your users/clients/customers. Therefore there are different dynamics in play. If I sell you a tool and I know it could be vulnerable, but I don't try and find out what those vulnerabilities are, then you're ultimately the one on the hook when all your data gets deleted or leaked.

2: Be periodically updated (in case of security bugs)
